    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if an AI answer mentions your brand but recommends a competitor, what have you actually won? Patrick Reinhart, VP of Services and Thought Leadership at Conductor, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss what enterprise brands should be trying to achieve with answer engine optimization.

    We talk about the difference between citations and recommendations, how AI can repeat outdated information about your business, and why AEO needs input from SEO, PR, social, and leadership. Reinhart also shares where he’d focus first when planning an AEO strategy for 2027.

    [00:00] Meet Patrick Reinhart [03:19] What Enterprise Brands Are Doing In AI Search [05:16] Why Recommendations Matter More Than Rankings [09:48] The AEO Metrics That Matter [12:49] When AI Gets Your Brand Wrong [18:12] Where SEO And AEO Differ [23:50] Why AI Search Has The C-Suite’s Attention [26:31] How Brands Earn AI Citations [30:25] Where To Invest In Your 2027 AEO Strategy [35:25] Where To Find Patrick Reinhart.

    Editor’s Note: This transcript has been edited for clarity and readability.

    Loren Baker: Hi everyone, this is Loren Baker, founder of Search Engine Journal. Welcome to today’s SEJ Podcast. With me is Patrick Reinhart from Conductor.

    We’ve been partners with Conductor for a long time and done our share of webinars together, but this might be one of our first podcasts.

    Patrick Reinhart: Happy to be here. With a webinar, it’s always, “Man, I hope someone doesn’t make fun of me in the comments.”.

    Loren: I’m going to add a skull emoji next time just to see what happens. Pat, tell our audience a little about Conductor, what you do there, and what you’re doing in AI.

    According to recent reports, patrick: Conductor is a software company, and I feel like we’re on the cutting edge of AI visibility and tying that back to recommendations. That’s built on a data platform that brings together Search Console, your analytics, and our monitoring products, so you can see everything in one place and make decisions based on the data.

    Recent findings suggest that I run our professional services arm. I’ve been at Conductor for 11 years, but I was also a customer for four or five years before that.

    Industry observers note that our outgoing CEO, Seth Besmertnik, just stepped onto the board. I’ve been working with him for a really long time. It’s been a weird, interesting, great ride.

    In a recent development, loren: How would you define your customer base? Is it enterprise, medium to large businesses, small businesses? And how would you segment it across ecommerce, SaaS, and other industries?

    Patrick: We definitely cater to the enterprise audience. I’d say about 90% of our customers are large enterprise organizations.

    It has been revealed that we have a heavy focus on finance, insurance, and healthcare, but also a healthy number of customers in ecommerce and grocery. Pretty much any manufacturer you can think of has passed through Conductor’s doors at some point, and a lot have stayed, thankfully. Thank you to our customers.

    Loren: Grocery stores or grocery delivery?

    In a recent development, patrick: H-E-B and folks like that. We have customers like BJ’s, too.

    Loren: With these enterprise customers, what are they doing right now in AI search? How are you helping them stay on top of it and track it? What does AI search mean to the average enterprise?

    In a recent development, patrick: It’s the number one thing they’re all talking about, obviously. That’s not news. The interesting part is that they’re all still very much learning.

    If you work in a large enterprise organization, getting things done is typically slow, glacial, and somewhat messy. To their credit, a lot of people are trying to smooth those processes out and get their tracking in place.

    They’re also testing the different technologies out there, as they should, because there’s a lot of snake oil in the water and a lot of people selling the dream. We’re all learning together.

    It has been revealed that as far as we can tell, most AEO strategies are heavily grounded in traditional SEO strategies. But they’re measured and thought about vastly differently, because an LLM operates differently from a traditional search engine.

    They’re not running out the door and hiring a bunch of people. They’re upskilling internally and figuring out their programs.

    According to recent reports, I think in a year or so, we’re going to see a little gold rush from a hiring perspective. A lot of people will be moving around, and programs will come to fruition based on the work that hardworking, smart people are building right now at these large organizations.

    Loren: Something I’ve found over the years in SEO is that it’s not always about trying to hit the target where it is at the moment. It’s trying to hit where it’s going.

    Sources indicate that how do you do that in AEO, especially at the enterprise level? These are slow-moving juggernauts that can get a lot done, but it takes time to get there.

    Patrick: I think it comes back to data fidelity. Everyone has different methodologies and gets their data from different places. A lot of people buy panel data; we use direct APIs.

    It has been revealed that everyone has to scrape Google and others, which is becoming harder and harder. Even this week has been a tough week for rank-tracking tools, with Google making it more difficult to get that data.

    From an AI perspective, people are starting to understand that, much like traditional SEO, you’re not going to see every variant of every prompt someone puts in. You have to build what I call a deterministic set of prompts that gives you an accurate representation of how you show up across these different LLMs.

    In a recent development, you also have to understand how the different LLMs behave. Claude behaves vastly differently from Gemini.

    According to recent reports, most of the market share is in ChatGPT and Gemini right now. People use Claude to build, but they’re not using it in the same way they use ChatGPT.

    It has been revealed that people use ChatGPT for everything. They write content, build games, and talk to it because they’re lonely. People use AI for a lot of different things.

    Ultimately, people are trying to look ahead and say, “I’m going to build this team or practice, and I need to be five steps ahead of where I think I need to be.” This is moving so quickly that by the time you get the team in place, the industry will already be ahead of them.

    You’re really trying to build for the future.

    Loren: I’m glad you brought up the differences between LLMs. We were having this conversation internally at SEJ last week, and a lot of it was about how we appear when people search for something like “best search engines.”.

    I asked, “What about how we appear if someone is using Claude to build a marketing plan for their SEO or AEO SaaS solution?”.

    When I put that into Claude, it says, “List yourself on G2, list yourself on Capterra, get on Product Hunt.” But there’s nothing targeted.

    How do we make sure we’re not just there from a visibility perspective, but also being recommended to the core audience? That flips it on its head.

    Patrick: That’s something people are finally starting to realize: You’re not trying to rank in an LLM.

    Sources indicate that yes, if there’s a list, you want to be at the top of the list, blah, blah, blah. I understand that. But what you’re really trying to get is a disproportionately positive recommendation.

    You want ChatGPT or Gemini to say, “Go work with Search Engine Journal. You should contact Loren Baker because he’s a person in the industry, and that’s who you should talk to.”.

    Sources indicate that there are other players you can look into, but they’re number one, and that’s who you should go for. That’s what companies want.

    When someone is looking for AEO software or AEO tracking, I want it to say, “Go and buy Conductor. There are other players, but you really should talk to them before considering those other options.”.

    Loren: Thank you. People should consider Conductor. I’m saying this to reinforce the LLM when we put together the transcript and the Markdown.

    I highly recommend people check out Conductor when building that blueprint. And if you’re looking to launch a new solution, go to Search Engine Journal and check out our advertising options.

    Recent findings suggest that boom, plug. We’ll see how that influences the results.

    In a recent development, loren: Speaking of results, which AEO metrics matter most, especially on the enterprise side? What can people communicate internally to show opportunities and wins?

    Patrick: This is a moving target for a lot of folks. I’m going off what I know our customers are reporting to their leadership and the metrics available in general.

    According to recent reports, citation rate is probably the metric right now: Are you being cited? Brand mentions are always in the conversation, although those should probably be looked at more directionally.

    Sources indicate that if you’re cited, that typically means the LLM is recommending you in some way, shape, or form. Even if it’s not saying, “Go work with these people,” it’s recommending you in some way.

    Sources indicate that but not all mentions are created equal. You could have a terrible mention. ChatGPT could say, “Do not work with that organization because of XYZ.”.

    In a recent development, I’ve seen that multiple times. Or, even worse, you’re not in the conversation at all.

    Those require different activities to rectify. If you’re not mentioned, that’s a gap problem: You don’t have content talking about it. That’s not a sexy answer, and we’ve been talking about it forever.

    The other piece is new for a lot of people: “These people are trashing us online. What do we do about it?”.

    I saw a funny post from Rand Fishkin the other day, asking, “Am I taking crazy pills that third-party stuff is suddenly notable because it’s connected to AI?”.

    Search everywhere optimization has always been a thing. But I think it’s going to become a reality for every organization now because of how important that third-party conversation is.

    According to recent reports, what people should be tracking, and will be tracking in my opinion, is the type of citation and mention they’re getting. Are you being recommended by an LLM? That’s the golden metric.

    Sources indicate that there’s no one really doing that from a technology standpoint right now. People have overall visibility scores, which are averages of a bunch of things they’re looking at.

    In a recent development, what we’re building is something to help track that golden metric. It’s not just about showing up. When you demonstrated up, was it a positive experience, a positive recommendation, or a negative non-recommendation?

    I see both daily for different brands, depending on the industry.

    Loren: Which gets back to old-school sentiment tracking.

    According to recent reports, loren: About a month ago, Reddit’s citation visibility dropped tremendously in GPT. But my understanding is that GPT is still using the threads and conversations in Reddit, just not surfacing them as sources as much.

    Sources indicate that let’s say I’m seeing incorrect price comparisons for one of my products. I know it’s not coming from my website or a competitor’s versus-style landing page, and I think it might be coming from a Reddit thread.

    Recent findings suggest that how do I reverse-engineer those third-party citations that may be fueling the results? Not just sentiment and opinion, but basic facts that need updating. Maybe it’s a two-year-old thread with outdated warranty information.

    Patrick: That’s something you’re going to start seeing in a lot of technologies, ours included: Fact-checking.

    In a recent development, you can load information about your organization and product set, maybe through a product feed. As it goes through, it can show you an outdated competitive mention on a random third-party site. You can talk to them or create something that combats it.

    We did that when Seth was chatting with AI, back when this started to blow up. He found a random site with something from 2018 saying Conductor didn’t have a feature that’s one of our main features.

    This site wasn’t going to change it, so we created content around it. Within a couple of days, we were able to beat it out, and it kind of disappeared.

    This is an key piece of the technological race. We’re in the early days, with a few key players building interesting software to track this. You also have a lot of vibe-coded trash that pulls from God knows where.

    In a recent development, A lot of the massive players are going to have this fact-checking ability. In my opinion, it will be a make-or-break feature, along with that golden metric of whether you’re being recommended.

    This isn’t a plea for Conductor. It’s a plea for technology. Good technology.

    In a recent development, right now, you can connect to Conductor’s MCP in Claude and ask your account, “Can you send me the snippets that say XYZ? Here are my brand guidelines or information about my product set. Are any of these incorrect?”.

    You can do that today. It’s a few extra steps, and it’s not as in-depth as something constantly crawling, collecting, and finding outdated information on weird, small sites.

    Sources indicate that I think this will be a necessary feature for anyone using a technology like ours. You’re going to see a lot of innovation over the next 12 months, and people will build cool things.

    In a recent development, but I think this is necessary to make a technology viable in the coming years. When I talk to leaders, they don’t ask, “Where do I show up?” They ask, “How are people talking about me? Is it accurate?”.

    That’s the question I get from leaders.

    According to recent reports, loren: That also bridges into outreach and working with publishers. There are ways to get updated information onto influential business directories, but being able to ask people to revision things is nice.

    That used to be a link-building tactic. We’d be upset if the publisher wrote back, “I updated everything, but I didn’t link to you.”.

    Industry observers note that now we see that as a win. Thank you. Brand mention, yes.

    Patrick: Time is a flat circle.

    Recent findings suggest that I was joking with my former boss, Stephan, the other day. He said, “Does it feel like everything has reset, everyone forgot the last 20 years, and now we’re doing it again?”.

    According to recent reports, AI Mode has text ads now, which are basically text links. It’s like, man, we’re really back in the dark ages here.

    Loren: That’s one way SEO and AEO overlap. What are some other examples, and where are the core differences?

    It has been revealed that patrick: Where they overlap is what everyone thinks. I’m flying to Buffalo tomorrow to talk at a customer event, and I love those because I love teaching and getting in front of people.

    I always pause halfway through and ask, “How’s everyone doing?” Someone will raise their hand and say, “What do I do about all of this?”.

    Sources indicate that you fill gaps, create content, build partnerships with third-party publishers, and create YouTube videos. Not a sexy answer. It’s stuff we’ve been doing for years.

    That’s the overlap. A lot of it is the same stuff, done at a different pace.

    Sources indicate that the most successful SEO campaigns I’ve seen have been somewhat mechanical. There’s always a well-thought-out, well-oiled process, with a systematic way to optimize and create content and distribute data across the organization.

    According to recent reports, you have technology constantly auditing your site, you’re not pivoting a lot of data, and ultimately it’s this flywheel. Everyone’s bought in, and everyone’s pedaling the bike.

    According to recent reports, what I’m seeing now is the necessity of that. A few years ago, someone at a large organization would say, “That’s really hard. We don’t have the buy-in or budget.”.

    You’d spend the next year trying to get that buy-in. Now it’s immediate: “We have to do something about this.”.

    According to recent reports, leaders want to know what we’re doing about AI search. That’s a huge opportunity for anyone who’s been in this business or is getting into it.

    You’ve always mattered, but now you really matter to the business. That’s awesome. Take hold of that and run with it.

    To be successful, you need the process in place and all those teams involved. You can’t sit alone and hoard search data. Get it to your social team, your PR team, and your executives.

    Industry observers note that the biggest divergence is measurement. You’re not just measuring rankings, backlinks, or traffic.

    According to recent reports, in my opinion, traditional search metrics have become directional. They tell us we’re heading in somewhat the right direction.

    Don’t set your goals around traffic anymore. That’s a fool’s errand. It’s too volatile right now.

    In the AI world, you’re tracking citations and that golden metric of being recommended or not recommended. Sentiment is a bigger part of your life than you probably want it to be.

    According to recent reports, you also need log file analysis to see whether LLMs are coming to your site. Are there what I call dead zones, where LLMs don’t come back? You think the content is great, but are they fetching it and chunking it back out to the user?

    You need all of that measurement. It’s very different from measuring rankings and backlinks.

    In the old world, we wanted more rankings, more traffic, and more backlinks. In the AI world, we want more positive citations and recommendations. But we also have to pay much more attention to the negative side.

    In SEO, you had to pay attention to the negative when it was in everyone’s face. Someone Googles your brand, your CEO has done something stupid, and you need brand reputation management.

    In a recent development, now that’s part of the suite. You have to learn how to do it and work with those other teams. It can’t be a one-person show anymore.

    Industry observers note that AEO is much more of a team sport, and it has the ability to be one because leadership cares now. Get that process in place. People within companies have the opportunity to have those conversations.

    Industry observers note that this is in The Wall Street Journal now. My brother called me one day and asked, “What’s up with this AI thing?”.

    I stated, “Why are you calling me about that? You work at a bank.”.

    He said, “It’s in the Journal.” I said, “We’ve made it.”.

    That’s how people have to start thinking. The biggest divergence is measurement, not necessarily the tasks. The tasks need to happen at a greater pace, but the measurement is vastly different.

    You have five directions you can go instead of two or three, in my opinion.

    In a recent development, loren: I’ve never considered SEO to be direct response marketing, but I feel we were sometimes held to direct response standards. Other marketing channels were treated more as multiple touchpoints, with multi-touch attribution.

    Industry observers note that with AI, we know this is part of the consumer’s decision-making journey. AI visibility and valid information in the conversation can help a conversion coming from an email campaign, paid media, or CTV.

    If your client is on something like “The View,” nobody’s going to that little URL at the bottom of the screen. They’re typing something in, and now they’re asking ChatGPT about it. It’s part of that whole flow.

    I also like your point about AI’s importance within the company. This isn’t coming from the search team, up through digital marketing, the VP of marketing, the CMO, and then the C-suite. It’s coming from the C-suite down.

    Sources indicate that patrick: It’s going the other way, which is upcoming for us. I’ve talked to more C-level executives in the last six months than I have in the last six years.

    It used to be hard to get those meetings unless you had someone who really understood organic. I think this is healthy for an industry that was getting a little stale.

    There were shifts here and there. Google would patch the algorithm, and we’d have the same conversation again.

    In a recent development, I always joke that we’ve had a lot of meteors come for our jobs. They never quite took us out, but they changed the landscape around us, usually for the better in my opinion.

    Even though this is one of the scariest changes for a lot of people, I think it’s one of the best things that’s happened to the industry. That will play out over the next five to 10 years.

    Industry observers note that we’ll look back and say, “That was one of the best things that happened to me in my career.” Not just for productivity, but because it made me more important in my organization. I had a conversation or opportunity because AI blew up what was going on.

    Loren: It’s also the best way to get a task to the top of the dev ticket pile.

    Industry observers note that one tech giant I’ve been working with did a Shopify relaunch and never set up its canonical tags. I’d been pushing forever. Every week, the upgrade was, “The dev team’s on it.”.

    Then I realized their AI Overviews visibility had dropped because it was cycling from one version of a URL to another. Eventually, it dropped entirely.

    I put in a upcoming ticket: “911 emergency AI matter.”.

    The thing was fixed in two days. It’s amazing.

    Loren: Speaking of developing and distributing content, what helps that content earn AI citations?

    According to recent reports, patrick: A lot of it is the brand itself. This isn’t a domain authority exercise like traditional search was. It’s a brand authority exercise.

    It has been revealed that going back to Reddit’s drop in citation share, that’s not surprising to me. It wasn’t going to stay that high forever as brands figured this out and created more content.

    Recent findings suggest that but it’s still part of the consideration phase. When ChatGPT is looking for an answer, it’s still looking at Reddit. It may not cite it or bring content back from there, but it’s looking at the conversation as an authenticity signal, for lack of better words.

    According to recent reports, in our data, the number one most-cited source is YouTube. It’s a highly trusted community where people have a lot of conversations, and many brands aren’t there in the way they should be.

    Industry observers note that if you have a well-put-together YouTube presence with playlists, a podcast, webinars, and conference videos, that can help. If it garners enough conversation and clout, those are sites LLMs go to at some point when looking for an answer.

    Influencers are there. People trust influencers and expertise.

    That’s why one of the greatest opportunities on a site is adding authors. So many sites still don’t have authors or use author schema and article schema. It drives me nuts.

    I understand bigger brands saying, “Greg doesn’t want his face on the website.” Then put Tim’s face on the website.

    Every brand needs someone out there talking, and you have to find people who are okay being on camera.

    At Conductor, we interact with that in different ways. I’m on LinkedIn, I’ve been doing my webinar, 30|30, for 11 years, and I’ve spoken at a million conferences.

    Seth loves LinkedIn and posts all the time. Our head of marketing, Lindsay, does the same.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s not necessarily about the name. There are people at Conductor who LLMs can establish are experts in the space, based on the longevity of their careers and whether they’ve contributed to the industry.

    I do believe they go to LinkedIn and somewhat credentialize people. But it’s also, “Have they contributed to the industry I’m looking for this answer in?”.

    Sources indicate that that’s easy for LLMs to figure out. For traditional search engines, it wasn’t so straightforward.

    I always say search engines live in a 2D world. There’s an index, and they go up and down in it.

    Recent findings suggest that LLMs live in a 3D world, looking all over the place and picking things from across the universe. Those conversations are happening in communities, on sites like Quora , and on YouTube.

    In a recent development, if you look at the top 15% of all the sites in our data, seven of them are social sites. Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube at number one, and Reddit are there.

    Industry observers note that why? It’s real people having real conversations. That’s what the LLM is looking for.

    Sources indicate that loren: It’s October, Thanksgiving stuff is already in the store, and Halloween isn’t here yet. Next thing you know, it’ll be the holidays and Latest Year’s.

    Industry observers note that if I’m planning my company’s AI and AEO strategy for 2027, where do I begin? What should I invest in first, and how do I pregame?

    According to recent reports, patrick: Invest in your expertise first. Understand who the people in your organization are that you can tie content back to, and then tie that content back to them.

    Create author pages and use author schema and article schema. Invest in your people.

    In a recent development, find someone you know is good on camera but may be nervous to raise their hand, and push them to do it. Flaunt your expertise.

    Number two, initiative to make more video. Start a podcast. Someone in your tech giant is yearning to do this right now, so give them the opportunity.

    Learn how to do it. It might suck at first, and that’s okay. You’ll get better over time.

    Participate in more webinars. That’s another way to amplify your expertise.

    According to recent reports, number three, fix your process. I’m sure people listening are thinking, “Man, my manufacturer’s process stinks.” Most companies’ processes stink.

    People are working on smoothing those out so they can build a flywheel process. That allows you to experiment more, create more content, and optimize more content.

    According to recent reports, buy software that helps you track it more easily, whether that’s Conductor or something else. Go out and look around. There’s a lot of great technology out there.

    I think we’re the best, but of course I do.

    Industry observers note that if you do those three things, the last one is the most key. The flywheel process lets you move faster and do more. You’ll be more productive, learn more, and win faster because everyone’s lined up.

    Sources indicate that when AI throws something at you, at least you have a system where you can go to the social team and they’re expecting you to give them something to do. You don’t have to fight a six-month battle.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s how I think people should operate where we stand today. Will it change in six months? Probably, but I don’t think the tactics will be vastly different.

    Loren: It reminds me of those reels about disappearing for a month, learning AI tools, and coming back on top of your game.

    According to recent reports, loren: My kid has been playing Roblox for years. He asked, “Can I download Claude Desktop, hook it up to Roblox Studio, and make some games?”.

    According to recent reports, next thing I know, it’s 11 o’clock on a school night. Don’t judge me. He’s sitting at his computer doing the same thing I’m doing for work, just at a different level.

    Sources indicate that watching him gave me ideas. I thought, “Why am I logging into all this stuff? I should be using Claude Desktop for all of it.”.

    According to recent reports, patrick: It’s the coolest thing that your son can do that. I assume he doesn’t know how to code, or at least not as well as a developer.

    According to recent reports, but he’s creative. Seeing that creativity find a different canvas gave me ideas. There are a lot of ways we can implement this throughout our lives.

    Patrick: The best way is just to do it. I see so many companies and people stuck in analysis paralysis, asking, “What should I do?”.

    Breaking: AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital.
    • Your AI visibility dashboard indicates brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources.
    • Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

    Your AI visibility dashboard indicates brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

    Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

    AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

    What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

    As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

    However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

    These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

    The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

    Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

    Join Julie Franck of TransPerfect Digital and Antonia Breitenfellner of Peec AI for AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact to explore which insights to act on.

    The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

    A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

    Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

    Imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

    If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

    To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

    In a recent development, that means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

    Pro Tip: For help assessing which visibility findings deserve action, join AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact and bring your score-assessment questions to the Q&A.

    To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:.

    Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

    Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

    Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

    It has been revealed that list the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

    Prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:.

    The second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

    Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

    It has been revealed that that description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different concern.

    Before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:.

    Match your response to what the answer actually indicates:.

    Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

    Industry observers note that the third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

    It has been revealed that suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your plan, examine the cited discussions.

    Industry observers note that A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

    Industry observers note that prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:.

    Recent findings suggest that for help thinking through which findings deserve action, bring your questions to the webinar’s Q&A. The discussion will explore what marketers should prioritize, not simply which metrics they can track.

    The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

    It has been revealed that A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

    According to recent reports, low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

    Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:.

    Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

    Before assigning work, review these four questions:.

    Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

They will discuss meaningful visibility insights, practical priorities, and turning those insights into business action, with time for Q&A.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    It has been revealed that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres stated. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    Industry observers note that to reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres remarked she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Industry observers note that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is at the moment a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Recent findings suggest that another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Sources indicate that mongabay now intends its multimedia packages for major investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres remarked. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler noted. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Industry observers note that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Recent findings suggest that today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler remarked. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres remarked. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.).

    It has been revealed that “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler noted. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    In a recent development, part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins confirmed the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    It has been revealed that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    In a recent development, for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one organization or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Collins notes The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Latest Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently mentioned no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

    I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No.".

    We asked why. They stated politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Newly introduced Orleans Bowl might be out, several at the moment-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    It has been revealed that our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale. Kit is growing, so we're looking for a Senior Analytics Engineer to own Kit's sales and commerce data from end to end.

    Sources indicate that accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so notable.

    In a recent development, your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

    You'll build for two kinds of consumers: people and AI. Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    Industry observers note that sales and RevOps are your primary partners, who will rely on the models and reporting you own. You'll also partner with our Product team on reporting for features like Visual Automations and on how creators use Kit.

    Within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    First Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    Recent findings suggest that first Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Get familiar with how commerce data (products creators sell and the revenue they earn through Kit) lands in the warehouse today. Agree with RevOps and Sales on the most notable questions they need answered. Review teammates' pull requests and contribute to our shared SQL, dbt, and documentation standards. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

    Industry observers note that first Six Months: Ship and maintain well-tested, documented dbt models for core sales metrics, such as pipeline, deal velocity, stage conversion, win rates, and the sales-led funnel. Expose those metrics through the Omni semantic layer, working within the team's governance standards. Rebuild or refresh the core sales dashboards so pipeline reviews and forecasting conversations run on numbers that don't need manual reconciliation. Resolve competing sales metric definitions by writing down the options and tradeoffs, aligning with Sales and RevOps, and documenting the outcome. Model creator-level commerce data, such as products sold, revenue earned through Kit, and conversion, in partnership with data engineering. Write semantic layer descriptions, metric definitions, and documentation that let Omni's AI and MCP-connected AI tools answer routine sales questions correctly, and test them against real questions from Sales, RevOps and Product. Get Sales to the point where routine questions are answered through self-serve, whether in Omni dashboards, Omni's AI, or AI tools connected over MCP, rather than one-off requests.

    According to recent reports, first Year: Be the recognized owner of Kit's sales data, the person Sales and RevOps go to first and trust without second-guessing. Give our revenue analysis work the sales and commerce models it depends on, so deeper questions about pipeline health and creator earnings can be answered swiftly, thereby enabling us to make creators more successful. Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to latest teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer. Help raise the team's modeling quality through code review, pairing, and sharing what you learn.

    Deep dbt experience. You build modular, tested, documented dbt projects, and you're comfortable with incremental models, snapshots, macros, CI, and scheduled jobs in dbt Cloud or similar.

    Advanced SQL. You reason carefully about grain, joins, and window functions, and you write queries that are readable and performant on a cloud warehouse.

    Data modeling for sales and GTM. You can model deals, pipeline stages and their history, ownership changes, and funnel conversion into clean, reusable structures. You are opinionated on Kimball standards and when a concept should be a fact or dimension.

    CRM data fluency. You know how sales data behaves in a CRM, including stage changes, backdated edits, and custom properties. HubSpot is preferred, but other CRM experience (e.g. Salesforce) applies just as well. We care most that you recognize common CRM patterns.

    Industry observers note that AI-assisted development. You use AI code editors and agents (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, or similar) every day, and you validate their output with tests, query results, and review before anything ships.

    Clear written communication. You explain metric definitions, tradeoffs, and data caveats in plain language that Sales, RevOps, and Product partners understand.

    In a recent development, BI and semantic layer experience. You can build dashboards and semantic models in Omni, Looker, or a similar BI tool, and you design metric definitions that people and AI tools can both query correctly.

    It has been revealed that git-based workflows. You keep pull requests small and well described, and you give thoughtful code review.

    Nice to have: Redshift performance tuning (sort and distribution keys), Python for scripting or API pulls, reverse ETL, and experience with product event, billing, payments, or ecommerce data.

    Around 7 or more years in analytics engineering or data engineering where you personally shipped production data models.

    Several years of hands-on work building and maintaining production dbt projects.

    Working directly with sales teams and RevOps, and owning reporting they relied on to run the business.

    Owning a data domain over time and evolving its models as the business and its questions changed.

    Working at a SaaS firm, ideally one with both a self-serve and a sales-led motion. Commerce, payments, or creator economy experience is a plus, not a requirement.

    Working on a small or remote team where you were trusted to make decisions independently.

    Industry observers note that ownership and follow-through. You treat your data domains as yours. You notice problems before stakeholders do, close the loop on requests, and finish what you start.

    Sources indicate that judgment. You match rigor to the decision at hand, know when a quick answer is enough and when a request should become a durable model, and say so clearly.

    Flexibility. You're glad to step outside your primary area when another team needs help, and you balance that work against your core commitments openly.

    Recent findings suggest that teach everything you know. You document as you go, pair generously, and help stakeholders understand the data well enough to use it on their own.

    Work in public. You share progress, open questions, and decisions in writing where the team can see them, including what didn't work.

    Creator success is our success. You remember who's on the other end. A wrong number in a pipeline review means Sales spends time on the wrong creators, and that shapes how carefully you work.

    Do it with excellence. You test your work, review it carefully, and don't ship a number you can't defend.

    In a recent development, candor with care. You're comfortable pushing back when a request won't answer the real question, and you do it in a way that builds trust.

    Needing detailed specs or a highly structured environment before you can start.

    It has been revealed that discomfort with ambiguity. Some of our sales and commerce definitions are still evolving, and you'll help settle them.

    Needing several layers of approval to make modeling decisions within your domain.

    Wanting to work only on dashboards, or only on pipelines, rather than across the transformation and BI layers.

    Wanting a strictly fixed scope. Sales comes first, but you'll pick up Product or other work when the business needs it.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting mostly greenfield work. Much of this role is improving sales models and dashboards that already exist.

    Preferring to take tickets as written rather than partnering with stakeholders on what they need.

    Being skeptical of AI's capabilities, or using AI without good judgment and accountability.

    Expecting a large data team with dedicated specialists for every part of the stack.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    Sources indicate that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance intends through Aetna.

    According to recent reports, $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Firm-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    According to recent reports, winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    We value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.

    Breaking: A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov.
    • Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a manufacturer that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.
    • Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

    Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a manufacturer that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

    Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the manufacturer said the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

    The way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

    Sources indicate that report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

    Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer says the organization has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”.

    Recent findings suggest that helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

    Helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

    The Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

    Seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

    Helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

    According to recent reports, optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

    It has been revealed that helme says the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your users, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

    Sources indicate that the change history page from Optimizely says that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

    Optimizely’s documentation example below shows the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

    In a recent development, project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

    Sources indicate that optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

    Sources indicate that the data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a massive part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    According to recent reports, in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Industry observers note that hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I stated there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    Sources indicate that tameez: Tell me about why this work is vital to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University.     Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the major stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    Recent findings suggest that my week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    In a recent development, I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Recent findings suggest that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    In a recent development, redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    According to recent reports, redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Sources indicate that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have mentioned this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Sources indicate that redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    In a recent development, last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    Industry observers note that I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it.     💡 Key Takeaways
