    • Industry observers note that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

    Sources indicate that I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

    Industry observers note that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post noted what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how significant it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

    Here is the entry for the November 2026 core enhancement, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

    Industry observers note that google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it said it changes Search thousands of times a year and introduces the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t revealed at all. So a named revision is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

    The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

    The date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

    What neither of them shows is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

    That hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November enhancement within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

    The closest thing I know to a core enhancement is the annual performance review.

    Sources indicate that anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

    Sources indicate that A core revision is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

    It has been revealed that the comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core update you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

    The strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

    According to recent reports, there’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content update to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who notes most affected sites had it coming.

    It has been revealed that look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the issue, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

    Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

    Most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and launched.

    Industry observers note that when that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an update window and gets blamed on the update.

    Sources indicate that then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

    This is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

    So there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the revision coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

    This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

    Recent findings suggest that take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation says it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

    The traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

    It has been revealed that “JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

    If quality is a list of items to tick, then a core upgrade is a latest edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

    So people who hold quality as a checklist need each update explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

    The first question a business could ask after an upgrade is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

    In a recent development, now read the PDF from the upgrade before. It indicates the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

    According to recent reports, the second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site rolled out.

    The fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

    Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

    In a recent development, the line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no update, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

    In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

    It has been revealed that google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account customers.

    On Thursday, the tech giant took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an enhancement to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    In a recent development, meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting newly introduced commercial terms into effect.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not blueprint to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    Sources indicate that in the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan.
    • In a recent development, I found this out the practical way.
    • According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan. 1, 2027. You may have deleted it because you don’t advertise in Europe. Don’t assume you’re off the hook. Google bills these surcharges based on where your ads are actually served, and its default location setting can serve your ads to people who have never set foot in your target area.

    In a recent development, I found this out the practical way. I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account. His campaigns are built to reach shoppers within a few miles of his store. On the morning of Nov. 11, his account received two notices from Google Payments, one headed “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in Italy” and the other “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in France.”.

    According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on. Then I went back, because I suspected plenty of Search Engine Journal readers were asking the same question I was. Why is a neighborhood retailer in Latest York getting billing notices about two countries he isn’t targeting?

    The short answer is that the emails are a warning, not a bill. Whether they become a bill depends on settings most local advertisers have never opened.

    According to recent reports, google calls these charges jurisdiction-specific surcharges. Some are labeled Digital Services Tax (DST) fees and some are labeled Regulatory Operating Costs, but they work the same way. They are added to your invoice on top of your ad spend, and on top of any account budget you set.

    In a recent development, here is how the rates for Google Ads stand on Google’s help page, before and after Jan. 1, 2027.

    Sources indicate that two former entries are off the list. Google notes ads served in India stopped carrying a 2% charge on Sept. 1, 2024, and ads served in Canada no longer carry the 2.5% DST fee.

    The same increases apply to Display & Video 360, and Google’s help page says YouTube placements bought on a reservation basis carry the surcharges too.

    In Italy, the jump is half a point. In France, it is a full point, which means the fee itself rises by 50%. Turkey moves the other way.

    See also: Ask A PPC: How Will The Tariffs Impact My PPC Campaigns?

    According to recent reports, google’s help page states the rule plainly. The charge applies every time an ad is served in one of these jurisdictions, “regardless of where your actual business is located.” The surcharge is calculated on the impressions or clicks served in each country, so an account that serves nothing in France pays nothing in France.

    That would seem to settle it for my client. But a few paragraphs further down, Google adds a warning that you might show ads to people in a country you never targeted “because your business is in a location of interest for them.” Google also notes it is the advertiser’s responsibility to make sure campaign target settings are correct, and that it will not refund surcharges triggered by legitimate clicks and impressions served according to those settings.

    In plain English, if your settings let a shopper in Milan see your ad, you pay the Italy surcharge on that impression, and you don’t get it back.

    See also: 13 Google Ads Settings To Check When Running International PPC Campaigns.

    Google’s advanced location options give you two choices for who counts as being in your target area. “Presence or interest” reaches people who are in, regularly in, or who’ve shown interest in your targeted locations. “Presence” reaches only people who are in or regularly in them.

    In a recent development, presence or interest is the default, and Google labels it as recommended. Google supports that recommendation with its own data, saying advertisers in travel, real estate, and education who switched to it saw 5% more conversions on Search campaigns. That is Google’s claim from Google’s internal data, and it covers three verticals, not retail.

    Recent findings suggest that for a store on Madison Avenue, “interest” is where Europe gets in. Someone in Paris searching for shops on the Upper East Side has shown interest in Latest York. Under the default, your ad can serve to that person, and the impression lands in France.

    According to recent reports, the controls have also been widening. Demand Gen campaigns picked up the same Presence or interest versus Presence choice in late 2025, and AI Max for Search has added options for reaching people based on locations of interest. More automation in where ads go means more chances to serve impressions in places you didn’t pick.

    Giovanni Perilli, a funnel marketing consultant who writes about European ad costs, published a breakdown the same day the emails went out. The France email he received did not mention Italy at all. In his words, the email “leaves out the change that matters most to anyone advertising in Italy.”.

    That matches my own experience, with a twist. My client’s account got two separate emails, one per country. Advertisers who received only one should check the help page rather than assume nothing else changed.

    Perilli also turns the surcharge into numbers a PPC manager can use. Because the fee is added on top of what you spend, he multiplies a cost-per-acquisition by 1.03 and divides a return on ad spend by 1.03. A €40 CPA effectively becomes €41.20. A ROAS of four becomes about 3.88. If your break-even ROAS is 2.5, your real target in France and Italy is now about 2.58.

    Those are small numbers. On thin retail margins in the first quarter, they are not nothing.

    See also: Google Says Changing tCPA & Budgets Won’t Reset Learning – 6 BFCM Takeaways.

    Google’s help page claims the France and Italy charges cover part of the cost of complying with digital services tax legislation in those countries. The tax news over the past year lines up with that.

    According to recent reports, french lawmakers voted in October 2025 to double France’s digital services tax from 3% to 6% for the largest platforms, but the budget bill carrying it was rejected a month later, and the rate remains 3%. Italy’s DST has applied at a 3% rate since 2020, and its 2025 budget law removed the domestic revenue threshold that had kept some companies out of scope. Turkey went the other direction, cutting its DST from 7.5% to 5% this year and to 2.5% on Jan. 1, 2027. Google’s Turkey surcharge falls to 2.25% on the same date.

    Google also has organization now. Meta began charging its own location fees on July 1, 2026, at 3% in France, Italy, and Spain, as Bloomberg reported. From January, Google and Meta charge the same 3% in all three countries.

    Industry observers note that here’s my read. Digital services taxes were sold to voters as a way to make big tech pay. The platforms are now itemizing those taxes on advertisers’ invoices, and some of those advertisers are small businesses on another continent. Whatever you think of the policy, the bill has moved down the chain, and PPC managers are the ones who have to explain it to clients.

    Here are four steps I’m taking in my client’s account, and I’d suggest you take them in yours.

    I almost ignored these notices, and I’ve been reading Google Ads billing emails since 2003. My advice is to treat them as an audit prompt, not as spam. The surcharge itself is modest. The real story is how many local accounts may be serving ads in Europe without anyone deciding they should.

    My client’s ads are meant for the Upper East Side, not Paris or Milan. I’d rather confirm that in a report before Jan. 1 than discover it on a February invoice.

    Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    A new study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    According to recent reports, A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less crucial — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    Recent findings suggest that that truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how key the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty latest. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    According to recent reports, “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.”.

The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    #43627. 6.9% Of ChatGPT Conversations Indicated Purchase Intent In U.S. Panel via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1181 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    6.9% Of ChatGPT Conversations Indicated Purchase Intent In U.S. Panel via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that brands have some insight into how often purchase intent reveals up in chat with ChatGPT, based on its presence in 6.9% of conversations in a U.S.
    • Sources indicate that data was provided by Verso, which tracks owners’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account.
    • Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that brands have some insight into how often purchase intent reveals up in chat with ChatGPT, based on its presence in 6.9% of conversations in a U.S. opt-in panel analyzed by SparkToro.

    Sources indicate that data was provided by Verso, which tracks owners’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account. The sample size is 41,961 conversations, generated by 12,321 people between Jan. 1 and Oct. 29, 2026. Most of the figures are from a sub-sample which had been statistically weighted to match the demographic characteristics of the U.S. population.

    Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business. Based on the analysis, Rand Fishkin (co-founder and CEO of SparkToro) concluded that the primary reason AI visibility matters is Google’s implementation of AI Overviews and AI Mode, rather than ChatGPT itself.

    Based upon the purchase-intent graph developed with the weighted group, there are three types of conversation by purpose. In a total of 4.9% of conversations, the person planned to purchase and was continuing to look at the options; another 2.1% were asking questions related to purchasing a specific brand, product or service; while a total of 93.1% revealed no intention to purchase.

    Fishkin wrote, “I suspect this is bad news for ChatGPT’s advertising opportunities.”.

    He also referenced SparkToro’s December 2024 analysis of approximately 332 million Google searches. He wrote that 15% or more of searches fit his definition. SparkToro did an analysis of searches done by a U.S. panel via browsers from January 2023 through September 2024. Commercial (a financial, business services or commerce intent) accounted for 14.5% of searches, although the searcher may not have been ready to make a purchase at that time.

    Transactional accounted for 0.69%. These categories do not match the categories identified in the ChatGPT graph which measured purchase intentions, so the percentages cannot be compared directly.

    In addition to tracking whether people asked about brands, the report also tracked if ChatGPT’s responses named any. In the weighted group, 86.7% of all prompts did not ask for brand, product or company information. Of all prompts, 6.6% asked about several brands, with the remainder being about a single brand (6.7%). On the response side, 7.0% of all responses mentioned multiple brands, products or companies while 5.1% mentioned one; the post’s reported percentage of responses mentioning at least one was 12.1%.

    The post’s takeaways describe 12% of ChatGPT usage as part of the buyer journey, though its purchase-intent chart puts conversations with purchase intent at 6.9%.

    Images and visual design requests were the top ranked category in the report with a total of 17.6% of conversations. Information and entertainment came second in terms of overall conversations (14.4%), writing and communication third (12.7%), while shopping, brands and local services made up 5.3%.

    In a recent development, one category per conversation was assigned, representing the primary goal of each. The output type counts over the topic when someone asks ChatGPT to create something (e.g., if you ask it to write an email asking for a refund from PayPal, that would be categorized as writing instead of shopping).

    It has been revealed that the percentages shown in the report’s chart vary from the percentages shown in the report’s text by less than two percentage points per category. The percentages provided here reflect the report’s chart.

    Recent findings suggest that the panel was also compared to OpenAI’s Signals data for September using the weighted group. OpenAI’s data was heavier towards writing and tech support, while the weighted panel data leaned more toward image requests and how-to questions. The author states the two are fair to compare given that OpenAI almost certainly includes API requests (that Verso does not track) in its numbers.

    Industry observers note that according to OpenAI’s page, the dataset “reflects only messages within ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, and Pro accounts” and Codex and enterprise usage are excluded from this count; thus excluding API calls as well. In addition, OpenAI presents global message shares whereas the panel indicates shares of U.S.-based conversations.

    Recent findings suggest that verso offers a free tool that breaks down a person’s ChatGPT history. Its sign-up terms say Verso stores the imported conversations and includes them, de-identified, in datasets it licenses to research and business customers. According to the post, Verso co-founder Aaron Aknin reached out to the post’s author and supplied the data.

    In a recent development, the report also described the panel as skewed toward younger people, women and people at lower income levels. There were 9,675 members in the panel that had demographic information that could be used as a weighting base to match the 2024 United States Census. No usage category varied by more than 1.4 percentage points when the demographics were weighted to these standards.

    In a recent development, before the data analysis was performed, the 131 heaviest people, who generated an average of over 33 prompts per active month, were eliminated. These heavy users accounted for approximately 1% of the total number of panelists, but they were responsible for sending 21% of all prompts. On average each member of the weighted group (excluding the above noted heaviest users) sent 9.9 prompts between January and October.

    As most panelists were recorded on mobile phones, the post says this may have caused some of the usage through desktop computers and work accounts to be underreported. API requests are not included in the data set.

    According to recent reports, each conversation was coded using a written code book provided to Anthropic’s model called Claude. Each conversation was coded based upon its title, up to six of the user-generated prompts, the initial few lines of ChatGPT’s first few responses and any product cards or bolded names. A second coder independently recoded a random sample of conversations, and the two coders agreed on categories 90% of the time and on brand tags 97% to 99% of the time. The post reports no separate agreement figure regarding its identification of purchase intent.

    SparkToro sells audience research software.

    According to recent reports, for brands splitting AI visibility and ad budgets, the U.S. panel gives a measured share of ChatGPT conversations that involve buying, and it’s under 7%. Fishkin concludes that Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode are what make AI visibility notable, and he questions whether tracking ChatGPT visibility is worth it unless Bing rankings and AI visibility are tracked too.

    According to recent reports, the post explains that the panel reflects what people ask ChatGPT much better than how often they use it. For PPC teams exploring ChatGPT Ads, the 6.9% purchase-intent share offers a snapshot of the conversation mix in a consumer panel with light ChatGPT use, not a count of purchase-related conversations across ChatGPT.

    Recent findings suggest that until panel data includes desktop, work and API use, it’s best to pair purchase-intent figures like this one with your own ChatGPT referral and ad data before adding them to a budget blueprint. Fishkin also shared that he looks forward to doing more research with Verso.

    Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    It has been revealed that “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    We’re hiring an Account Executive to own Australia and Latest Zealand across our commercial and enterprise segments.     Handle data residency, security, and procurement conversations with enterprise and public sector buyers.

    Hand off to Customer Success so customers onboard well and expand.

    5+ years in a technical sales role, ideally selling developer tools, databases, cloud infrastructure, or open source.

    A record of consistently beating quota, with numbers you can walk us through.

    Experience closing both fast moving commercial deals and longer enterprise cycles with procurement, security, and legal involved.

    Enough technical fluency to hold a credible conversation with an engineer without bringing a Sales Engineer to every call.

    Comfort selling to founders, CTOs, and platform teams.

    Strong judgment about where to spend your time across a territory spanning two countries and several time zones.

    Self-directed, at ease with ambiguity, and happy to build the playbook as you go.

    Experience with Postgres, or a competing backend or database platform.

    An existing network across the ANZ startup, scale-up, and developer ecosystem.

    Experience with cloud marketplace or co-sell motions, particularly AWS.

    Familiarity with ANZ compliance expectations, such as Australian Privacy Act, NZ Privacy Act, or financial services and government requirements.

    You’ll sell a product developers already love, with real inbound demand and a fast growing open source community behind it. The territory is yours, the ownership is real, and the team is small enough that your ideas get used rather than filed.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    It has been revealed that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Recent findings suggest that once a year, the entire organization gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Sources indicate that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📖 Baca

    Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance.
    • Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests.
    • CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance. They also share that attempts to control crawler traffic can sometimes accidentally block Googlebot and harm Search visibility.

    Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests. Google’s automated crawling systems interpret the improved performance as an indication that more crawling is possible and responds by gradually increasing the crawl rate.

    CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.

    According to recent reports, when Google increases the crawl rate, the initial crawl is handled by the origin server. But now Googlebot is hitting the server more aggressively and it’s this that can overwhelm the origin server, initially.

    Sources indicate that “For one, suddenly the crawling metrics suggests the site can handle a larger amount of crawling. And on the flip side, because the CDN caches aren’t yet populated, the origin server still has to serve the requested pages.

    Basically, CDNs take the valve off the hose, so now crawlers are drinking from a fire hose.”.

    Cherry Prommawin added more details:.

    According to recent reports, “Under normal circumstances, our crawlers operate under an notable rule. When a server responds faster, the crawlers assume the infrastructure is healthy and slowly ramp up crawl speed.

    Recent findings suggest that …So the crawlers see how fast the server responds, get really excited, and start to crawl the entire site at a higher, higher, and higher speed. But it’s a trap.

    People assume a CDN can catch a crawl spike from day one, but …The cache has to be filled up with the assets off the site first.”.

    Gary Illyes explained that on a first request for a page the CDN has to fetch the page from the origin server first to populate the cache with the content. It’s not until the second request for the page that the cache is populated with the content and begins doing its job.

    According to recent reports, “…which means your origin server may get slammed by the flood anyway. Now, to be fair, our crawlers take time to ramp up. It won’t happen in a millisecond.

    It has been revealed that an empty cache means your origin server is still doing all the heavy lifting. Until that cache is populated, your CDN isn’t acting as a shield just yet.”.

    Industry observers note that A CDN cannot serve an un-cached URL without retrieving it first from the origin server and that only happens after a request for that URL is first made. Crawlers visit large numbers of URLs virtually all the time and can generate a substantial amount of origin traffic before the CDN’s caches are fully populated.

    This next concern involves accidentally blocking Googlebot and triggering a reduced search presence because Google can no longer crawl and index URLs from a website. Illyes and Prommawin explain it in the context of a website admin flipping a switch at Cloudflare and inadvertently blocking Googlebot.

    Sources indicate that this is a real problem, I recall an instance in which a popular website’s massive traffic dried up whenever Cloudflare was activated and would return once they turned it off. They had a devil of a time diagnosing why this was happening and the customer service people at the time were unable to help them. It may have been the case, as Illyes and Prommawin noted, that the admin had turned on a strict bot filter that inadvertently blocked Googlebot.

    Illyes offered an example of an admin doing exactly that:.

    “They look at the spiking traffic, assume they are being aggressively scraped by botnets, and naturally, they panic.”.

    And what sometimes happens next is that an admin might turn on “blanket security rules” that block Googlebot.

    Prommawin offered more details:.

    …If the CDN detects automated requests, it intercepts them with a CAPTCHA challenge, asking them to click pictures of traffic lights to prove they’re human.

    It has been revealed that …It sees automated requests, flags it as a bot, and then intercepts with a CAPTCHA. And since our crawlers cannot identify a traffic light, they fail the test.”.

    What eventually happens with prolonged Googlebot blocking is that Google will begin dropping the pages from the index.

    Sources indicate that prommawin suggested that site admins should configure their CDN to allow known and trusted crawlers. This is a method called whitelisting where only crawlers that are on the “allowed” list can get it and all other crawlers cannot.

    They also recommend the use of CDN-level rate limiting of Googlebot if the requests on the origin server lead to downtime which can negatively impact legitimate human traffic to the website.

    Recent findings suggest that when a site initially starts out with a CDN, the CDN does not have a cache of a website’s content. The cache doesn’t get loaded until it’s requested by a browser or crawler visit.

    Cache pre-warming is the process of requesting content from a site so that the content gets loaded onto the CDN. This ensures that the content is already loaded onto the CDN before owners request it, which ensures that the content is delivered quickly without the CDN having to first retrieve it from the origin server (the server where the actual content files exist).

    Illyes recommends “pre-warming” the cache by programmatically requesting URLs from it so that thE cache is populated in a controlled manner.

    “And to survive augmenting your site with a CDN, see if you can pre-warm the caches by programmatically fetching your top URLs through the CDN before you open the floodgates to search engines.”.

    Google’s main point is that moving to a CDN can create an unexpected combination of faster crawling and increased origin-server demand. That in turn can lead to unintentionally setting aggressive security restrictions that prevent Googlebot from accessing a website.

    Three especially notable points for SEOs and site owners:.

    1. Using a CDN can trigger an increase in Googlebot crawling when it detects faster server responses, even though the CDN’s caches have not yet been populated, which in turn means an increase in requests for URLs from the origin server.

    Industry observers note that 2. A CDN migration can inadvertently cause pages to disappear from Google Search due to aggressive security settings intended to stop malicious bots can also lock out Google’s crawlers.

    It has been revealed that 3. Google recommends pre-warming caches, allowing trusted crawlers, and temporarily controlling crawling when server demand becomes excessive.

    Read Google’s fresh CDN documentation here.

    AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    For our newly introduced report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries mentioned they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) mentioned they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Recent findings suggest that our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more swiftly.

    “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) remarked they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    Sources indicate that using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    In a recent development, as AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    Recent findings suggest that this also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several notable questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    In a recent development, first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    It has been revealed that second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also indicates that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    Recent findings suggest that the differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a upcoming dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Sources indicate that expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    Industry observers note that this doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    Recent findings suggest that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    Recent findings suggest that as pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules.

    #43613. Tech Report: Google Ads AI Max Is Making More Decisions For You – Here’s What To Audit Now via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.
    • According to recent reports, campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026.
    • In a recent development, google indicates the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.

    According to recent reports, campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026. Dynamic Search Ads will follow in February 2027.

    In a recent development, google indicates the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings. However, AI Max also brings additional controls and optimization options that advertisers have the option to enable.

    For PPC managers, this is a good time to review which decisions Google is already making, which settings are active in your accounts, and whether those settings are aligned with your business goals.

    Here’s what to audit before giving AI Max more control over existing Search campaigns.

    Before changing anything, it’s crucial to understand how AI Max is currently configured across your accounts, if at all.

    Industry observers note that google’s migration process doesn’t enable every AI Max feature automatically for every campaign. The settings depend on which legacy functionality each campaign was using.

    According to Google’s migration documentation:.

    This is why it’s worth checking each campaign, because two campaigns showing AI Max as enabled may have very different levels of automation running.

    According to recent reports, within Google Ads, review the AI Max settings at both the campaign and ad group levels. Specifically, check whether search term matching, text customization, and Final URL expansion are active.

    Search term matching can be controlled at the ad group level, while text customization and Final URL expansion are campaign-level settings.

    I’d also look at whether any campaigns have different configurations than expected, especially those that were recently migrated or created using Google’s default settings.

    Recent findings suggest that the goal here is to establish what’s running before making additional changes. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to evaluate which AI Max features are influencing performance.

    Search term matching is one of the areas I’d spend the most time reviewing, especially in campaigns with tightly defined keyword strategies.

    AI Max can use broad match and keywordless matching technology to identify additional searches based on existing keywords, ads, and landing pages.

    While it can help campaigns reach relevant searches that weren’t covered by the original keyword list, it’s also notorious for introducing traffic that doesn’t fit the campaign’s intended purpose.

    Research from Mike Ryan at Smarter Ecommerce (SMEC) shows how much AI Max can expand beyond an advertiser’s existing keyword targeting.

    In an analysis of 383 million impressions, Ryan found that more than 25% of impressions attributed to exact match keywords in AI Max-enabled Search campaigns came through AI Max search term matching.

    Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t mean those searches were necessarily irrelevant. However, it does show why advertisers shouldn’t assume exact match keywords are limiting traffic to their original targeting.

    Google’s AI Max reporting documentation outlines additional reporting fields that can help advertisers understand how searches are being matched.

    When reviewing Search terms, I’d focus on:.

    Competitor searches might deserve some extra attention, based on Ryan’s research.

    In SMEC’s research, Ryan documented one account where competitor searches accounted for 69% of total Search impressions.

    That’s a single-account example, but it highlights how heavily the traffic mix can lean toward searches outside the advertiser’s original targeting.

    I also wouldn’t judge every latest search term solely by whether it converts immediately.

    Some campaigns may have some wiggle room to support earlier-stage research, especially when there’s enough budget to fund it without taking away from stronger existing demand.

    However, if a campaign is already struggling to capture its highest-intent searches, expanding into more informational traffic might be worth excluding for the time being.

    Negative keywords remain available with AI Max, along with brand controls and ad group-level locations of interest.

    Text customization allows Google to generate additional headlines and descriptions using existing ads, keywords, and landing page content.

    For advertisers already using automatically created assets, the audit should focus on what’s being generated and how those assets are performing.

    Google’s optimized asset reporting provides additional performance metrics, including spend and conversions, to help advertisers evaluate the assets being served.

    I’d look closely at three areas:.

    A generated headline could be technically accurate for the business but inappropriate for the campaign’s audience.

    This deserves additional review in industries with legal, compliance, or partner messaging requirements.

    Sources indicate that google allows advertisers to review and remove generated assets. It has also introduced AI Brief and text disclaimer controls to provide additional guidance over generated messaging.

    According to recent reports, see also: Should You Use Auto-Generated Creative? – Ask A PPC.

    There’s another consideration for campaigns that rely on responsive search ad pinning.

    Google’s AI Max documentation confirms that pinning isn’t always respected when Final URL expansion is enabled.

    Recent findings suggest that when Google selects a different landing page, it may generate ad copy that better matches that destination rather than using the advertiser’s pinned assets. Pinning also isn’t respected when URL inclusions are provided.

    For campaigns with required disclaimers, pricing language, or partner-approved messaging, I’d check whether the current settings support those requirements.

    If pinning is essential, Google recommends avoiding Final URL expansion and URL inclusions.

    When Final URL expansion is enabled, Google can select a different landing page from the advertiser’s website based on the search query.

    That may help when a website has several relevant product or service pages, but it can also create problems when the destination doesn’t align with the campaign’s goals.

    A website might contain informational articles, support documentation, and pages promoting services outside the campaign’s intended focus.

    Those pages could be relevant to someone’s search, but not something worth spending PPC dollars on.

    Google’s landing page and search term reporting can help identify which URLs are receiving traffic through AI Max.

    For lead generation, I’d also look beyond the initial form submission.

    According to recent reports, A landing page might generate more leads while attracting more unqualified customers. That can be difficult to identify without qualified lead or sales data.

    Google supports URL exclusions at the campaign level and URL inclusions at the ad group level.

    Those controls can help advertisers limit where traffic goes without necessarily turning off Final URL expansion across an entire campaign.

    For accounts with tightly controlled conversion experiences, I’d review the available URLs before enabling broader expansion.

    See also: Should Your PPC Strategy Focus On The Lead Pipeline Or Revenue?

    Google has reported that advertisers using the full AI Max feature suite see an average of 7% more conversions or conversion value at a similar CPA or ROAS compared with using search term matching alone.

    That figure comes from Google’s internal 2026 data for non-retail advertisers, and it shouldn’t be treated as an expected result for every account.

    Independent research from Smarter Ecommerce offers another perspective.

    In a March 2026 analysis of more than 250 campaigns, Mike Ryan found that AI Max generated a median 13% more conversion value relative to the remaining campaign revenue.

    However, those conversions came at a median CPA that was 16% higher than the campaign baseline.

    ROAS results also varied considerably. While the median difference was 0%, individual campaign results ranged from 42% above baseline to 35% below it.

    Sources indicate that these figures come from observational campaign data rather than controlled experiments measuring incremental performance. Ryan also noted that the analysis couldn’t account for potential cannibalization across campaigns.

    The research doesn’t mean AI Max is underperforming across the board. It suggests that additional conversion volume may come at a higher cost, with results varying significantly between accounts.

    If broader matching is reaching more informational or earlier-stage searches, those users may need more time before converting. Some may never become customers.

    According to recent reports, for lead generation, I’d compare the quality of conversions coming through AI Max against existing traffic. Are those leads qualified? Are they turning into opportunities or customers?

    For ecommerce, revenue, ROAS, margin, and the products being sold can provide more information than conversion volume alone.

    Google has expanded its AI Max experimentation tools, including the ability to maintain brand and location controls during testing.

    For campaigns that haven’t fully adopted AI Max, experiments can help compare performance before enabling additional functionality.

    I’d avoid changing several settings at once because it’s more difficult to attribute performance swings to a particular feature set of AI Max.

    If the goal is to understand whether broader matching improves performance, structure the test around that decision. The same applies to Final URL expansion or text customization.

    Google’s experiment setup has eligibility restrictions, so not every existing campaign can use the same testing approach.

    For campaigns already migrated with legacy functionality enabled, reviewing current performance may help identify which settings are worth testing next.

    Advertisers still running Dynamic Search Ads have time before Google’s automatic migration begins in February 2027.

    Industry observers note that google indicates the migration will convert dynamic ad groups into standard ad groups while preserving supported legacy settings and data. Its upgrade documentation also notes that unsupported legacy DSA targets may become read-only.

    I’d review existing dynamic ad targets, URL exclusions, and search term performance before the transition.

    Some campaigns may contain targeting decisions that made sense when they were created but haven’t been revisited recently.

    For advertisers with complex websites or large inventories, confirming which pages and services should remain eligible is worth doing before the migration.

    I wouldn’t approach this audit by immediately turning off AI Max features or adding restrictions across every Search campaign.

    Some accounts may benefit from giving Google more flexibility to find relevant searches, customize messaging, and select landing pages.

    I’d start with campaigns where those decisions could have the greatest impact on performance or where existing controls serve a clear purpose.

    That includes campaigns with limited budgets, strict lead qualification requirements, regulated messaging, or carefully managed landing page experiences.

    For campaigns already performing well, reviewing current settings and reporting may be enough to determine whether additional testing is worthwhile.

    Recent findings suggest that as Google moves more Search functionality into AI Max, advertisers still have control over several notable decisions. Knowing what’s enabled, how Google is using that flexibility, and what results the business is receiving should guide where those controls are applied.

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.
